findings.claim: French trompette de la mort, trumpet of death, for its dark color only
findings.because: The dark color is only part of the story. French sources tie the name mainly to the mushroom coming up around All Saints' Day (Toussaint, 1 November), when the French remember their dead. It is not named for its color alone.
findings.fix: French trompette de la mort, for its dark color and All Saints' season

findings.claim: The death in its French name is for its dark color.
findings.because: The why of a trap has to be true. The name comes from the dark color and also from fruiting around All Saints' Day, the French day for remembering the dead.
findings.fix: The death in its French name is for its color and season. It cooks in minutes.

findings.claim: and they are hard to farm, hence the price
findings.because: This is out of date. Outdoor morel farming in China has grown large since the 2010s and now supplies much of the dried morel trade. Most fresh morels in Western kitchens are still foraged, and that is what keeps the price high.
findings.fix: and most are still foraged, hence the price

findings.claim: It's a big, ruffled mushroom that grows at the foot of oak trees.
findings.because: Menus almost always print this as maitake (the card's own line says "Crispy maitake"), so a new hire reading the menu will not connect it to the guest line. The line also suggests it was foraged under an oak, when most restaurant maitake is farmed, and that invites a follow-up the server cannot answer.
findings.fix: It's maitake, a big, ruffled mushroom that grows wild under oaks and is farmed too. Roasted, the frilly edges crisp up and the center stays tender and earthy.

findings.claim: (no say given, while the line reads "Crispy maitake, miso butter, charred scallion")
findings.because: The dish will be ordered as maitake, and a new hire will stop at that word. The term needs no respelling, but the alias the server actually says aloud does. The guest line above is one place to carry it.
findings.fix: my-TAH-kee (for Maitake)

findings.claim: Tight cluster of small caps on long stems
findings.because: A tight cluster of small caps on long stems is the defining picture of enoki, which is on the roster and in this card's seeAlso. Only the second half of the gist separates the two. Beech caps are the rounder, brown or white button caps, and that is the half to lead with.
findings.fix: Clump of round brown or white caps, bitter raw and nutty cooked

findings.claim: (no say given for Abalone Mushroom)
findings.because: New hires stumble over abalone and say it three or four ways. In American dining rooms it is ab-uh-LOH-nee.
findings.fix: ab-uh-LOH-nee MUSH-room

findings.claim: named for its chew, which is a lot like abalone. Seared, it's savory and buttery with real bite.
findings.because: Most guests have never eaten abalone, so comparing the chew to abalone tells them nothing. It also leaves the server saying the same thing twice (chew, then real bite). Comparing it to a food they know answers "what is that?" better.
findings.fix: named for the shellfish because it has the same firm, springy chew. Seared, it's savory and meaty.

findings.claim: "oyster mushroom", "often butter", "often garlic", "sometimes wheat flour"
findings.because: The card's notThis tells a shellfish-allergic guest "Not oysters, the shellfish", yet oyster mushrooms are classically stir-fried with oyster sauce in Chinese and Southeast Asian cooking. Oyster sauce is made from oysters, so a guest could hear "not oysters" and wrongly take it as clearance. The madeWith list has to flag it.
findings.fix: "oyster mushroom", "often butter", "often garlic", "sometimes wheat flour", "sometimes oyster sauce"

findings.claim: Not oysters, the shellfish. The name comes only from the shape of the cap.
findings.because: "The name comes only from" sounds like a promise that shellfish plays no part in the dish, when these mushrooms are often cooked in oyster sauce. The sentence should explain the name without implying the dish has no shellfish.
findings.fix: Not oysters, the shellfish. The name is for the cap's shape, though dishes may use oyster sauce.

findings.claim: "abalone mushroom", "often butter", "often garlic", "sometimes soy sauce"
findings.because: In Chinese cooking, abalone mushrooms are classically braised in oyster sauce, often as a stand-in for real abalone. The notThis line ("Not abalone, the shellfish") invites a shellfish-allergic guest to feel cleared, so the shellfish-based sauce needs to be flagged.
findings.fix: "abalone mushroom", "often butter", "often garlic", "sometimes soy sauce", "sometimes oyster sauce"

findings.claim: This is a mushroom that only borrows the name for its chew.
findings.because: "Only borrows the name" reads as an assurance that the dish has no shellfish. The classic preparation is braised in oyster sauce, which is made from oysters.
findings.fix: A mushroom named for its chew, though it is often braised in oyster sauce.

findings.claim: It is a choice edible that cooks in minutes.
findings.because: "Choice edible" is a foragers' term that says the mushroom is fine to eat. That is an edibility assurance about a wild mushroom, and correcting the trap does not need it. The real correction is that the "death" in the name refers to the color.
findings.fix: The death in its French name is for its dark color, not poison. It cooks in minutes.

findings.claim: Nearly all its value is aroma, which heat and time destroy, so it is shaved raw over warm, fatty food.
findings.because: This is true of white truffle, which is never cooked. Black winter truffle is routinely cooked gently in classic French cooking: slipped under poultry skin, folded into sauce Périgueux, infused in eggs or butter. Gentle heat in fat brings its aroma out. The card as written would have a server tell a guest that cooked black truffle is wrong.
findings.fix: Its value is aroma, which heat and time dull, so white is shaved raw and black warmed gently in fat.

findings.claim: a Japanese mushroom grown on oak logs
findings.because: Most shiitake sold to restaurants today is grown on sawdust blocks, not logs, and the card's own why says so. The mushroom is native to East Asia and was first cultivated in China. Only the name is Japanese.
findings.fix: an Asian mushroom grown on hardwood

findings.claim: Porcini are wild Italian forest mushrooms
findings.because: Porcini (king bolete) grow wild across Europe, North America and Asia, and much of the dried porcini sold is from Eastern Europe or China. Only the name is Italian, and a guest who asks where the porcini came from should not be told Italy by default.
findings.fix: Porcini are wild forest mushrooms

findings.claim: It's a Japanese mushroom grown on oak logs
findings.because: Most shiitake sold to restaurants is grown on sawdust blocks, not oak logs, so a server saying this at most tables says something false. The card's own why says logs or sawdust blocks.
findings.fix: It's a Japanese mushroom first grown on logs

findings.claim: We shave it fresh over the dish, and the smell is the whole point.
findings.because: This states a service practice as fact. Many kitchens fold truffle into a sauce or butter, or use preserved truffle, so a new hire who repeats this word for word can be wrong about their own dish. Hedge it.
findings.fix: It's usually shaved fresh over the dish, and the smell is the whole point.

findings.claim: It's a finishing oil with a strong truffle aroma. It's a big, earthy hit of that flavor for much less than shaved fresh truffle.
findings.because: Talking about price at the table sounds awkward, and the line suggests real truffle when the why says the aroma is usually manufactured. A guest who asks what it is should hear, honestly, that it is flavored oil.
findings.fix: It's an oil flavored to smell like truffle, drizzled on at the end. It gives a big, earthy hit of that aroma.

findings.claim: Truffle fries, parmesan, parsley
findings.because: A menu line has to carry the term or an alias as written. This one says only 'Truffle', so it teaches the Truffle card, not Truffle Oil.
findings.fix: Fries, truffle oil, parmesan, parsley

findings.claim: They make the richest mushroom risotto there is.
findings.because: This oversells, and it doesn't fit when the porcini on the menu is in pasta, on veal or in polenta. The guest line should hold up for any dish.
findings.fix: They're a classic in risotto and fresh pasta.

findings.claim: sears up tender and stringy
findings.because: 'Stringy' is unappetizing to say at a table and works against the sell. The honest selling point is the flaky, shredded texture, like crab.
findings.fix: sears up tender and flaky

findings.claim: tears like chicken
findings.because: The gist holds 'chicken', a word from the term itself, so on the test it gives the answer away and fails the term-free rule. The gate misses it only because 'chicken' is not on the banned list.
findings.fix: Orange shelf fungus off tree trunks that tears into meaty strands

findings.claim: Farmed mushroom fed on chicken manure, named for how it is grown
findings.because: Traps must be term-free like gists. 'Chicken' in the wrong option points straight at the term and makes the test easier than intended.
findings.fix: Farmed mushroom grown on poultry manure, named for how it is raised

findings.claim: (no note)
findings.because: This card is missing a real raw-service fact. Raw or undercooked shiitake can cause shiitake dermatitis, a documented itchy, streaky rash in some people, so it is meant to be cooked through. A server should be able to say so plainly.
findings.fix: Served cooked. Raw or undercooked shiitake can give a few people an itchy rash.

findings.claim: "cremini mushroom", "often butter", "often garlic", "sometimes thyme"
findings.because: The card's own menu line reads "Roasted cremini, garlic, thyme, sherry", but madeWith leaves the alcohol out. That list is the only place a guest avoiding alcohol would see it flagged.
findings.fix: "cremini mushroom", "often butter", "often garlic", "sometimes thyme", "sometimes sherry"

findings.claim: Always served cooked.
findings.because: This states the house practice as a guarantee a guest could rely on, and some kitchens do serve enoki raw in salads. The real fact is the handling rule: packaged enoki has been linked to US listeria outbreaks and recalls, so it is meant to be cooked through.
findings.fix: Cook it through. Packaged enoki has been part of US listeria recalls, so it should not go out raw.

findings.claim: "sometimes pork"
findings.because: The card's menu line is "Beef hot pot, enoki, napa cabbage, tofu", and enoki rolled in beef is a classic dish, but beef is not on the list. The line also names tofu, and soy is covered only as "often soy sauce".
findings.fix: "sometimes beef", "sometimes pork"

findings.claim: "lion's mane mushroom", "often butter", "sometimes garlic", "sometimes lemon"
findings.because: The pairs field sends the reader to "crab cake style with remoulade". A crab-cake-style lion's mane cake is classically bound with egg and breadcrumbs, and remoulade is a mayonnaise, so it is made with egg. None of these is flagged.
findings.fix: "lion's mane mushroom", "often butter", "sometimes garlic", "sometimes lemon", "sometimes egg", "sometimes breadcrumbs"

findings.claim: "sometimes wheat flour", "sometimes egg"
findings.because: The menu line is "Fried chicken of the woods, hot honey, pickles". The classic fried-chicken treatment soaks the pieces in buttermilk before the flour, so the list leaves out milk.
findings.fix: "sometimes wheat flour", "sometimes egg", "sometimes buttermilk"

findings.claim: Always cooked through, never raw.
findings.because: This states the house practice as a guarantee. The real fact is that the mushroom must be cooked through, and a few people react even to cooked pieces.
findings.fix: Must be cooked through. A few people get an upset stomach even from cooked pieces.

findings.claim: "fresh truffle", "often butter", "often egg", "sometimes parmesan", "sometimes cream"
findings.because: The card's menu line and its classic service are fresh egg tagliatelle, which is made with wheat flour. Wheat is not flagged anywhere on the card.
findings.fix: "fresh truffle", "often butter", "often egg", "often fresh pasta", "sometimes parmesan", "sometimes cream"

findings.claim: The gist leans on 'shellfish-like bite', and that is also what sets apart Lion's Mane ('sears up like crab meat') and King Trumpet ('seared like scallops'). In a multiple-choice test with those two as the other options, a reader cannot tell which fungus is the 'shellfish' one. The gist says nothing about what makes the abalone mushroom itself: a thick, dark cap in the oyster family.

It only works as a wrong option by being a different thing entirely. The mistake that really appears is in the packet ('soft, spongy quality, woodsy'): treating shiitake as a soft, mild mushroom.

critic.notes: Section checks otherwise pass. Every one of the 16 roster rows has a card. The section mean is 664 chars (ceiling 720). There are no banned substrings and no verdict words: 'free' appears only in 'trimmed to free them' on Beech, which is not verdict language. There are no em or en dashes. No two gists or guest lines are the same. No roster row carries a knownPacketError, so no trap is required for one. The confusable pairs are linked both ways: Hen of the Woods and Chicken of the Woods, Black Trumpet and King Trumpet, Truffle and Truffle Oil. Oyster Mushroom is linked to Oysters, and Truffle to Chocolate Truffle. Cross-section follow-ups for the operator: (1) check that fd_0255 Chocolate Truffle and fd_0115 Oysters link back to Truffle and Oyster Mushroom in their own confusedWithTerms. (2) King Trumpet could take seeAlso Scallops (fd_0118), because 'king oyster scallops' is a common menu name for it. (3) Chicken of the Woods has seeAlso 'Fried', but its line is 'Fried chicken of the woods', so fd_0002 Chicken-Fried is the closer related card and worth considering. (4) Truffle Oil's gist uses 'truffle', which the genericWords list permits. It is still the card's own head noun, so a mostly-truffle multiple-choice set could be easy. Acceptable as written.

findings.claim: "Burgundy Truffle"
findings.because: An alias must be another name for the same product. Burgundy truffle is the autumn crop of the same species (Tuber aestivum, formerly var. uncinatum). It is sold as a separate, darker, more fragrant and pricier product, which the card's own note says. Listing it as an alias tells a server that a Burgundy truffle supplement is the same thing as a summer truffle one. It also contradicts the gist's 'warm-weather' and the why's 'ripens from late spring'.
findings.fix: Drop "Burgundy Truffle" from aliases and keep the distinction in the note.

findings.claim: in Piedmont and central Italy
findings.because: Tuber magnatum is also dug commercially in Croatian Istria, Slovenia, Hungary and Serbia, and menus often print 'Istrian white truffle'. As written, the card reads as if Italy were the only source, so a server would be wrong-footed by a Balkan-origin supplement.
findings.fix: in Italy and the Balkans

findings.claim: is cooked only briefly, often in a clear broth or with rice
findings.because: In matsutake gohan, the classic rice dish the line itself points to, the mushroom steams with the rice for the full cooking time. It is handled gently to keep the aroma, but it is not always cooked briefly. The why's 'barely cooked' has the same problem.
findings.fix: is cooked gently, often in a clear broth or with rice

findings.claim: "sometimes soy sauce", "sometimes rice"
findings.because: Classic dobin mushi and matsutake gohan are both seasoned with light soy sauce and sake as a matter of course, so soy (and the wheat in soy sauce) is 'often', not 'sometimes'. Sake (alcohol) is missing entirely, and it matters more to a guest than rice does, which the guest line already names.
findings.fix: "often soy sauce", "often sake" (replace "sometimes rice")

findings.claim: for its pale, lumpy cap
findings.because: Why the mushroom is called sheep's foot is disputed. Sources credit a hoof-like cap shape, a woolly or velvety surface, or an older sense of 'pied'. The card states one reason as settled fact.
findings.fix: likely for its pale, hoof-like cap

findings.claim: It's shaved generously, so you get the look and flavor at a friendlier price.
findings.because: This oversells. A summer truffle has a fraction of the winter truffle's aroma (the card's own why says so), so a guest promised 'the flavor' at a lower price will feel misled. 'Shaved generously' is also a kitchen-specific promise the server can't guarantee, and 'friendlier price' is sales copy read off a card.
findings.fix: It's the black truffle of the warmer months. It's milder than the winter one, nutty and earthy, and it costs a good deal less.

findings.claim: It's the rarest truffle, dug wild in northern Italy each fall and shaved raw over your plate.
findings.because: 'The rarest' is a superlative the server can't back up, and white truffles are also found in central Italy and Istria (the card's own why says central Italy). The bigger floor problem is price: a guest who says yes to a by-the-gram shaving without being told gets a surprise at the check, and the guest line is what the server actually says.
findings.fix: It's Italy's prized wild fall truffle, shaved raw over your plate and priced by the gram.

findings.claim: "Burgundy Truffle"
findings.because: The card's note says the autumn crop sold as Burgundy truffle is darker inside and more fragrant. Listing it as a plain alias teaches a new hire to tell a guest that a Burgundy truffle is the mild summer one, which the note contradicts. Leave that fact in the note and take the name out of aliases.
findings.fix: ["Scorzone", "Black Summer Truffle"]

findings.claim: mild in scent and priced low
findings.because: A summer truffle is cheap only next to a winter truffle. It is still a costly supplement, so 'priced low' teaches a server to call it cheap. The gist is also 9 characters longer than the card's only trap, so it is the longest option.
findings.fix: Warm-weather black truffle, beige inside, milder and far cheaper

findings.claim: mat-soo-TAH-kee
findings.because: Under the key, 'mat' reads like 'cat', but American dictionaries (Merriam-Webster: mät-sü-TÄ-kē) and dining rooms open the word with 'maht'. The deck's own Shiitake card uses the same ending as shih-TAH-kee, so only the first syllable needs to change.
findings.fix: maht-soo-TAH-kee

findings.claim: It smells of pine and cinnamon and is cooked only briefly, often in a clear broth or with rice.
findings.because: At 166 characters it is well past the 150 aim, and the trailing list of generic uses is more than a nervous server can say smoothly at a table. Trimming it keeps the scent hook and the broth.
findings.fix: It smells of pine and cinnamon and is barely cooked, often in a clear broth.

findings.claim: soft little spines under the cap, hence the name.
findings.because: 'Hence' is written English. Read aloud by a third-day server it sounds read off a card, and naming the animal says the same thing more plainly.
findings.fix: soft little spines under the cap, like a hedgehog.

findings.claim: "matsutake mushroom", "often bonito dashi", "often sudachi citrus", "sometimes rice", "sometimes shrimp", "sometimes chicken", "sometimes soy sauce"
findings.because: The card's own menu line is dobin mushi with ginkgo, and the classic dobin mushi broth and matsutake gohan are both seasoned with sake and light soy sauce. The list leaves out alcohol (sake) and ginkgo nut, and it lists soy only as 'sometimes'. A guest who avoids alcohol or nuts would not see either flagged. Rice and chicken are the least important items for a guest with an allergy, so they can go to keep the list at 7 items.
findings.fix: "matsutake mushroom", "often bonito dashi", "often sake", "often soy sauce", "often sudachi citrus", "sometimes shrimp", "sometimes ginkgo nut"

findings.claim: "often egg yolk"
findings.because: White truffle is classically shaved over whole fried, scrambled or baked eggs as well as over yolk-rich tajarin. If the list flags only the yolk, a guest allergic to egg white (the more common egg allergy) could read it as saying the white is not there.
findings.fix: "often egg"

findings.claim: "sometimes rice"
findings.because: Rice is on the list because of white truffle risotto, which is classically started with white wine. The alcohol is not flagged, and the list has room for a seventh item.
findings.fix: "sometimes rice", "sometimes white wine"

findings.claim: Hedgehog Mushroom and Chanterelle are the classic look-alike pair. Both are buff to golden wild mushrooms of the same season, often sold and plated together (this card's own line and guest line put them side by side). But Chanterelle is only in seeAlsoTerms. The confusion the card does link, Lion's Mane, is the weaker one.

findings.claim: The note restates the card. "Priced by the gram" is already in both the gist and the guest line, and "autumn" and "fall" already give the season. The note adds only the October to December window, which is the kind of restating note the brief says to cut first. At 702 characters it is also the section's longest card.

findings.claim: The origin guesses at the etymology ("likely for its pale, hoof-like cap"). Rule 8 says to leave a fact out when it is not sure, and a server will repeat this reason as fact.
findings.because: The origin guesses at the etymology ("likely for its pale, hoof-like cap"). Rule 8 says to leave a fact out when it is not sure, and a server will repeat this reason as fact.
findings.fix: Drop the guessed reason: "French pied de mouton, sheep's foot, its name on French menus", or simply "French pied de mouton, meaning sheep's foot".

findings.claim: The why says "most now come from China, Korea and North America, where a close relative grows". It can be read as saying the Chinese and Korean supply is also a relative, when those countries grow the true species and only the North American pine mushroom is the close relative. The why is also 281 characters, above the 260 aim.

findings.fix: Rephrase to "so most now come from China and Korea, plus North America's pine mushroom, a close relative." This removes the ambiguity and trims the why toward the aim.

findings.claim: The level placement looks inverted. White Truffle is placed at level 4 (rare or specialist) while Summer Truffle is at level 3. On American menus the white truffle supplement is the one guests ask about by name every fall, and it is the more famous product of the two. The standard puts specialist products a senior server must know at level 3.

dispositions.reason: Dropped "Burgundy Truffle" from the Summer Truffle aliases. The note still says the autumn crop is sold as Burgundy truffle and is darker and more fragrant.
The White Truffle why now reads "in Piedmont, central Italy and the Balkans", so a Balkan-origin (Istrian) supplement no longer contradicts the card.

The guest line now says "is cooked gently" in place of "only briefly". The why now says the scent "fades with hard cooking, so it is torn and cooked gently, in broth or with rice" in place of "barely cooked", which fits matsutake gohan.
Soy sauce moved to "often", "often sake" was added and "sometimes rice" was removed, as part of the merged madeWith fix under safety-13.
The origin is hedged to "likely for its pale, hoof-like cap".
Replaced the guest line with the suggested honest one: milder than the winter truffle, nutty and earthy, and a good deal cheaper. It drops "shaved generously" and the promise of the same flavor.

The guest line now opens "It's Italy's prized wild fall truffle, shaved raw over your plate and priced by the gram". That drops the unbacked superlative and the northern-Italy-only claim, and tells the guest the price before they order.
The aliases are now ["Scorzone", "Black Summer Truffle"]. The Burgundy distinction stays in the note.

The gist is now "Warm-weather black truffle, beige inside, milder and cheaper" (60 characters). The comparative "cheaper" replaces "priced low". I cut "far" from the suggested fix so the gist is shorter than the 61-character trap and is no longer the longest option.
The respelling is now maht-soo-TAH-kee, matching American dictionary usage and the Shiitake card's ending.

Trimmed the guest line to end "is cooked gently, often in a clear broth" (147 characters). I kept fact-3's "cooked gently" in place of this fix's "barely cooked", because matsutake cooked with rice is not barely cooked.
"hence the name" is now "like a hedgehog" in the guest line.

madeWith now flags sake, soy sauce (often) and ginkgo nut. I dropped rice as suggested, but kept "sometimes chicken" and dropped "often sudachi citrus" instead, because a meat flag matters more to a guest than a citrus garnish, and sudachi is still on the menu line. The list stays at 7.
"often egg yolk" is now "often egg", so the flag covers whole eggs and the white, not only the yolk.
Added "sometimes white wine" as the seventh madeWith item on White Truffle, to flag the alcohol in the risotto.
Chanterelle moved from seeAlsoTerms into confusedWithTerms beside Lion's Mane, Black Trumpet kept in seeAlsoTerms, and notThis rewritten to tell both apart (132 characters).
Dropped the note that restated the price and season, taking White Truffle from 702 to 631 characters.
Removed the guessed etymology; origin now reads "French pied de mouton, meaning sheep's foot".
The why now says China and Korea, plus North America's pine mushroom, a close relative, so only the North American supply is called a relative; it is tightened from 290 to 278 characters.
White Truffle moved to level 3 beside Summer Truffle, because it is the specialist product guests ask for by name every fall, which the standard places at Sous Chef.

critic.notes:
I checked the whole section of 20 cards: 16 live and 4 new (fd_0321 to fd_0324). Every roster row has a card. No gist or guest line collides with another. None of the four new rows carries a knownPacketError. I found no banned words, verdict language or en/em dashes in the new cards. Traps stay within 10 characters of their gist, and the gist is never the longest option (White Truffle 64 against 67, Summer Truffle 60 against 61). Every madeWith list is under 140 characters joined. The section mean with the four new cards is about 661 characters of prose per card, well under the 720 ceiling. Each new card's total is 663 to 702.

Cross-links for the operator to consider, on existing cards this pass does not own:
(1) fd_0152 Lion's Mane has no confusedWith and no notThis. If fd_0324 keeps Lion's Mane in confusedWithTerms, Lion's Mane should link back to Hedgehog Mushroom, with a notThis such as "Not hedgehog mushroom, an ordinary cap with spines beneath. This is a shaggy white ball with no cap."
(2) fd_0148 Truffle Oil links to fd_0147 Truffle only. Its why names white truffle as the compound's source, so adding White Truffle (fd_0321) to its confusedWith would make the link go both ways.
(3) If fd_0324 takes Chanterelle as a confusion, fd_0141 Chanterelle (confusedWith currently empty) could link back to Hedgehog Mushroom.
(4) Neither fd_0147 Truffle nor any other card is specifically the winter black Perigord truffle, yet fd_0323's notThis leans on it. If the deck grows, "Black Truffle" (Perigord) would be worth promoting from the bench. The lexicon already has a black-truffle essay.
